list.listitem: Comprehensive injury reduction programs, work practices, engineering and environmental interventions may reduce the incidence of needlestick and other sharps injuries. B

At the time of a potential bloodborne pathogen exposure (BBPE), test the source patient for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, hepatitis B virus (HBV) active infection with surface antigen (HBsAg), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. C

Baseline and follow-up testing of exposed healthcare personnel (HCP) is required when a source patient is communicable for a bloodborne pathogen. HBV antibody testing is unnecessary if the HCP already has a documented immune status. C

Depending on source patient’s HIV status and risk factors, administer HIV post exposure prophylaxis (PEP) as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours. HIV PEP consists of a 3-drug regimen for 28 days which can be tailored for known or suspected antiviral resistance in the source patient. B
Depending on source patient’s HBV infection status and the exposed person’s HBV immunity status, administer HBV PEP as soon as possible. C
Workplace exposure to human blood or other potentially infectious material (OPIM) via percutaneous injury or via splash to a mucus membrane or nonintact skin.
Percutaneous injuries in healthcare personnel (HCP) generally involve contaminated sharp instruments such as needles, lancets, scalpels, bone fragments or broken glass.

OPIM includes vaginal fluid, semen, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, and amniotic fluid, and any fluid or tissue visibly contaminated with blood. Feces, saliva, urine, saliva and sputum are not considered OPIM unless visibly bloody.
Perinatal, sexual, and other nonoccupational BBPEs are not covered in this chapter.
The main concern after a potential BBPE is the transmission of HIV, HBV or HCV.

Other rare infections have been reported with needlestick injuries such as Blastomycosis, Brucellosis, Cryptococcosis, Diphtheria, Ebola virus, Herpes simplex, Leptospirosis, Malaria, Mycobacterium marinum, Mycoplasma caviae, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Syphilis, Toxoplasmosis, Tuberculosis, and Varicella zoster.
Direct transmission of bloodborne microorganisms from a source patient to the HCP.
Transmission is affected by the concentration and virulence of microorganisms, blood volume transmitted, and the immune system of the exposed person.
In the late 1990s, the CDC estimated that each year 385,000 needlesticks injuries sustained by US HCP in the hospital setting; an average of 1000 sharps injuries per day.
The magnitude of the problem is not accurately estimated due to limited participation in voluntary surveillance programs, lack of surveillance outside the hospital setting, and underreporting.

In US hospitals, the rate of sharps injuries is approximately 26.3 per 100 occupied beds per year. The most common setting for sharps injuries is the perioperative service, with 41.7% of sharps injuries. While overall sharps injury rates have fallen in the US since the Needlestick Injury Prevention Act in 2000, perioperative injuries have been increasing in recent years. Suture needles are the mostly commonly involved type of sharp instrument.
In US hospitals, splashes with blood/OPIM most commonly occur in the patient’s room. The rate of reported splashes is approximately half that of sharps injuries.

HBV is highly infectious and can remain viable on surfaces for up to 7 days. Estimates of risk for HBV transmission to unvaccinated HCP following a percutaneous exposure to an infected source range from 10 to 30%. However, widespread vaccination programs and routine use of PEP have reduced the risk of occupational HBV dramatically, such that the incidence of acute HBV infection in HCP declined 98% from 1983 to 2010.

The risk of HIV transmission from an occupational exposure is commonly cited as 0.3% and 0.09% for percutaneous and mucocutaneous exposures, respectively.
However, these estimations were based on data obtained prior to the widespread availability of highly active antiretroviral therapy, when viral loads of hospitalized source patients were often quite high, and before the routine use of PEP. More recent surveillance data suggest the risk in US hospitals is much lower; indeed there has only been one documented occupational HIV infection in the US since 1999.

Transmission rates are improving internationally as well. Among over 400 South Korean HCP who completed surveillance following a confirmed exposure to an infectious source over a 10 year period, there were no seroconversions.

Hepatitis C risk from a percutaneous exposure was initially estimated at approximately 1.9%. However more recent studies have found much lower transmission rates of 0.1 to 0.2%. With only two cases of occupational mucocutaneous transmission documented, transmission risk from a splash can only be described as exceedingly rare.
A study in 2016 estimated the median aggregate (direct + indirect) cost for needlestick injury to be around $747 (range, $199-$1,691).
The cost of HIV PEP medication and monitoring is approximately $4000 per exposed HCP.
Lifetime treatment costs for an occupationally-acquired infection in the US are estimated at $64,490 for chronic hepatitis C and $326,500 for HIV.

BBPE rates are highest among medical students, newly hired workers, house staff and other trainees.
Extended work hours are associated with exposure risk in registered nurses.

Transmission risk increases with the viral load of the source patient. In HIV patients, terminal AIDS correlates with higher risk of transmission. For hepatitis B, a positive hepatitis B e-antigen correlates with a higher viral load and greater infectivity of the source, although screening the source for presence of e-antigen is not recommended.
Injury circumstances that increase risk are visible blood on device, deeper injury, large-bore hollow needles, and exposure to a device that has been in a patient’s artery or vein.

Engineering and environmental interventions such as double gloving for high-risk procedures, special needle devices, safety syringes, and needle-less IV systems may reduce the incidence of needlestick injuries, although the quality of evidence is low.
Comprehensive multidisciplinary safety programs focused on reduction of BBPE can be effective in decreasing injuries among perioperative staff.

Work practices aimed at improving communication, such as communicating the planned sharps handoff method during a preprocedural safety checklist, can improve HCP's perceived safety during operative procedures.

The use of blunt rather than sharp needles for suturing muscle and fascia substantially reduces the risk of needlestick injuries among surgical staff. Use of blunt suture as the first line closure device for muscle and fascia is recommended by the American College of Surgeons, National institute for Occupational Safety and Health, endorsed by the Association of Perioperative Registered Nurses, and required by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA).

The OSHA Bloodborne Pathogen Standard requires that employers maintain a comprehensive Exposure Control Plan that includes ongoing identification, evaluation and selection of effective engineering controls such as safety-engineered sharps devices, as well as work practice controls to eliminate or reduce exposure.
HCP who may have contact with sharps or blood products should receive hepatitis B vaccine, followed by a test for HBsAb in 1 to 2 months.

Universal childhood hepatitis B vaccination started in the early 1990s, and now many HCP were vaccinated in infancy and lack record of a timely post-vaccination HBsAb. Most will have a low or undetectable HBsAb if tested in adulthood, but the vast majority will retain immune memory and mount a robust anamnestic response to a challenge with either vaccine or exposure to hepatitis B. Organizations may choose to document HBsAb upon hire, providing a challenge dose of vaccine followed by another HBsAb in 4 – 8 weeks for anyone with negative serology, or to check HBsAb at the time of a BBPE with conservative postexposure management of a negative HBsAb.
There is no effective preexposure prophylaxis for HCV or occupational exposure to HIV.

Immediately wash skin with soap and water or rinse exposed mucus membrane thoroughly with water. Do not use bleach or other caustic materials. There is no evidence to support the practice of expressing blood or fluid from the wound.
Expedite triage and obtain a history regarding exposure circumstances, source patient, and vaccination history of exposed HCP.

Test the source patient for HIV antigen (or combined antigen/antibody), hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), and hepatitis C virus (HCV).
Ideally the HCV test should be a nucleic acid test (NAT) for HCV RNA, but if this is not available an antibody test may be conducted, reflexing to a NAT if the antibody is positive. Obtaining the patient’s consent for testing may be required, depending upon applicable state laws and institutional policies.

A rapid HIV test is strongly advised to facilitate prompt decision-making regarding PEP. If the source patient is positive for HIV infection, or PEP is being prescribed, test the exposed person for HIV antibody at baseline.
If the source patient is communicable for HCV, test the exposed person for HCV antibody at baseline.

HIV PEP is indicated when the source patient is HIV-positive, regardless of viral load, when the source is at high risk or is clinically suspected to have HIV, or when a contaminated sharp from an unknown source raises a high level of concern, such as a needle from an HIV clinic. When indicated, PEP should be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within two hours of the exposure.

HIV PEP generally consists of a 3-drug regimen containing a dual nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) plus either an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), protease inhibitor boosted with ritonavir, or a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor. See for preferred and alternative PEP regimens. Recommendations are primarily based upon tolerance, convenience and safety. If the source patient is known to have drug-resistant HIV, PEP drugs should be tailored according to known drug susceptibility. Expert consultation is advised in this situation.

Expert consultation regarding HIV PEP is available through the National Clinicians’ Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Hotline (PEPline) at 888-448-4911. Seek expert consultation for PEP when the exposed individual has renal failure or hepatitis, takes medications that interact with PEP medications, is pregnant, or is considering delayed initiation of PEP beyond 72 hours when medication risks may begin to exceed the benefit.

Although there are no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) establishing a protective effect of PEP on HIV seroconversion, the best evidence for the effectiveness of HIV PEP comes from a case-control study found that cases had significantly lower odds of having taken zidovudine after exposure compared with controls (OR = 0.19; 95% CI, 0.06-0.52).

High quality human studies of HIV PEP regimens, such as RCTs, are unlikely to be conducted due to the ethical and legal obligation of employers to provide currently recommended PEP to exposed HCP. Data from controlled trials in animal models using simian immunodeficiency virus in macaques and HIV in humanized mice have found that rapid initiation of PEP and completion of a full 28-day course were much more effective than delayed start or shorter regimens. A systematic review and metanalysis of nonhuman primate studies found an 89% reduction in transmission with early PEP.

Hepatitis B vaccine is effective in preventing hepatitis B infection in health care workers, and the exposed person’s susceptibility to HBV infection may be determined based upon vaccination and post-vaccine surface antibody (HBsAb) or documentation of prior infection. Do not repeat the HBsAb if a positive post-vaccination HBsAb has been documented previously.

Depending on the source patient’s HBV infection status and risk factors, and on the exposed person’s HBV immunity status, administer HBV PEP with hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) as soon as possible according to .
Exposed health care workers who were previously infected with HBV, or who have positive serology for HBsAb following vaccination, do not need HBIG.

Use clinical judgement when considering HBV PEP with HBIG for exposure to an source whose HBV status is unknown. Source patients at low risk for HBV due to their country of origin and childhood vaccination status are unlikely to be communicable for HBV, and US-born HCP with documented childhood vaccination but a negative HBsAb separated more than 10 years after vaccination are likely immune.
Although there is no effective PEP for hepatitis C, early identification of infection is important because early treatment with a shortened course of direct-active antiviral agents may be indicated.
Counsel the exposed person regarding risk and transmission of specific blood-borne pathogens, including how to prevent future occupational exposure, and any indicated post exposure precautions.

During the follow-up period after exposure to any bloodborne pathogen, exposed persons should avoid blood or tissue donations. During the first 12 weeks following exposure to HIV (but not to HBV or HCV) exposed HCP should avoid pregnancy and breastfeeding if possible, and should use barrier contraception to prevent exposing a sexual partner.
HIV PEP should not be denied solely on the basis of pregnancy and breastfeeding. Expert consultation is advised in these situations, but PEP should not be withheld pending consultation.

An increase in neural tube defects among pregnant women in Botswana taking dolutegravir prompted global pharmacovigilance and extensive study. Global pharmacovigilance has not confirmed the association. In multiple large international cohorts evaluating pregnancy outcomes among HIV positive mothers, dolutegravir was not associated with neural tube defects.
Dolutegravir is recommended by the World Health Organization as a first line agent for HIV PEP, and in the US it is the preferred ART for pregnant women with HIV regardless of trimester.
Administration of prophylactic hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and initiation of the hepatitis B vaccine series are not contraindicated during pregnancy or lactation.
Monitor exposed HCP taking HIV PEP clinically for tolerance and adherence. Up to half of individuals discontinue PEP early, though newer regimens are quite well tolerated.
Individuals taking HIV PEP should be monitored with a complete blood count, renal and hepatic function tests, at baseline and 2 weeks.

Following HIV exposure, test the exposed HCP for HIV antigen and antibody by 4th generation assay at 6 weeks and 4 months post exposure. If 4th generation testing is not available, test the exposed HCP for HIV antibody at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and 6 months.
Following HCV exposure, test the exposed HCP for HCV RNA at 3 to 6 weeks, and HCV antibody at 4-6 months.
Following HBV exposure, if the HCP does not have immunity, repeat HBsAg and anti-HBs at 6 months.

Additional postexposure testing is indicated in certain unusual circumstances. Extend HIV testing to 12 months if the HCP contracts HCV from a source who was co-infected with HCV and HIV. Consider an additional HCV RNA test alongside the 4-6 month antibody test if the HCP is immunocompromised.
During follow-up appointments, assess the psychological impact of the exposure. BBPEs can be quite stressful, and exposed HCP may benefit from brief counseling.

Promptly refer any HCP with a newly identified bloodborne pathogen infection to a specialist for treatment. Bloodborne pathogen infections can be managed, and do not preclude a career in healthcare. Even with chronic infections, with appropriate management and maintenance of low viral loads, infected HCP can safely practice surgery, dentistry, medicine, or any allied health profession.

tr.th: Principles of HIV Post Exposure Prophylaxis

list.listitem: All PEP regimens include at least 3 drugs, regardless of exposure risk level.
PEP regimens are based on a “backbone” of two nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI/NtRTI) to which a third drug is added.

The third drug which may be an integrase strand transfer inhibitor, a protease inhibitor boosted with ritonavir, or a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, but should NOT be another NRTI/NtRTI.

tr.td: Prescribing details and standard adult dose
tenofovir DF 300 mg + emtricitabine 200 mg once daily. Combination available as Truvada®
tenofovir DF (Viread®) 300 mg once daily + lamivudine (Epivir®) 150 mg twice daily or 300 mg once daily
tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg + emtricitabine 200 mg once daily. Combination available as Descovy®
zidovudine 300 mg + lamivudine 150 mg twice daily. Combination available as Combivir®
zidovudine (Retrovir®) 300mg twice daily + emtricitabine (Emtriva®) 200 mg once daily.
Prescribing details and standard adult dose

Lopinavir 400 mg + ritonavir 100 mg twice daily. Combination available as Kaletra® which contains 200 mg lopinavir and 50 mg ritonavir per tablet. Prescribe two tablets twice daily of Kaletra for PEP.
Atazanavir (Reyataz®) 300 mg + ritonavir (Norvir®; RTV) 100 mg once daily.
Darunavir (Prezista®) 800 mg + ritonavir (Norvir®) 100 mg once daily.
